title: FULL OUTER JOIN
description: Learn how to use the FULL OUTER JOIN to return all rows from both left and right tables with matching rows where available.

data.alt: SQL Server full outer join with a WHERE clause example
SQL Server full outer join example
SQL Server full outer join - members table
SQL Server full outer join - projects table
SQL Server Full Outer Join illustration

data.text: The FULL OUTER JOIN is a clause of the SELECT statement that returns a result set including all rows from both left and right tables. When no matching rows exist for a row in the left table, the columns of the right table will contain NULL. Likewise, when no matching rows exist for a row in the right table, the columns of the left table will contain NULL.

data.title: FULL OUTER JOIN Syntax
data.content: Return all rows from both T1 and T2.
data.code:
SELECT
    select_list
FROM
    T1
FULL OUTER JOIN T2 ON join_predicate;

data.text: The OUTER keyword is optional, so you can use FULL JOIN instead of FULL OUTER JOIN.

data.title: FULL JOIN Syntax (Shorthand)
data.code:
SELECT
    select_list
FROM
    T1
FULL JOIN T2 ON join_predicate;

data.text: In this syntax, T1 is the left table and T2 is the right table.
Let's set up some sample tables in a project management (pm) schema to demonstrate the full outer join.

data.title: Create Schema and Tables
data.content: Create pm schema with projects and members tables.

data.title: Insert Sample Data
data.content: Insert rows into projects and members tables.
data.code:
INSERT INTO
    pm.projects(title)
VALUES
    ('New CRM for Project Sales'),
    ('ERP Implementation'),
    ('Develop Mobile Sales Platform');

INSERT INTO
    pm.members(name, project_id)
VALUES
    ('John Doe', 1),
    ('Lily Bush', 1),
    ('Jane Doe', 2),
    ('Jack Daniel', null);

data.title: Full Outer Join Between Members and Projects
data.content: Return all rows from both members and projects.
data.code:
SELECT
    m.name member,
    p.title project
FROM
    pm.members m
    FULL OUTER JOIN pm.projects p
        ON p.id = m.project_id;

data.text: The query returned members who participate in projects, members who do not participate in any projects, and projects which do not have any members.
To find the members who do not participate in any project and projects which do not have any members, add a WHERE clause.

data.title: Full Outer Join with WHERE for Unmatched Rows
data.content: Find members without projects and projects without members.
data.code:
SELECT
    m.name member,
    p.title project
FROM
    pm.members m
    FULL OUTER JOIN pm.projects p
        ON p.id = m.project_id
WHERE
    m.id IS NULL OR
    p.id IS NULL;

data.title: FULL OUTER JOIN vs UNION of LEFT/RIGHT JOINs
data.text: FULL OUTER JOIN is equivalent to a LEFT JOIN plus a RIGHT JOIN minus the INNER JOIN. It returns all rows from both tables.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables, with NULLs where no match exists.
Use WHERE IS NULL to find rows unique to either table.
Useful when you need a complete picture from both sides of a relationship.
